title: The Witch and the Whispering Falls
markdown:
Witch Briar lived in a crooked little cottage perched unsteadily on the side of the tallest blue mountain, as if the slope had agreed to hold it and then thought better of it. From her spot the world below looked like a rumpled emerald-green blanket. Tiny jewels of villages were scattered across it, thin silvery shepherd paths stitching them together. Her constant companion, and some might say her most critical judge, was Ink: a cat as black and sleek as a polished shadow. He seemed to have an opinion on everything, though he rarely said it aloud. Thoughts arrived as elegant tail-flicks, a subtle ear-twitch, or an occasional pointed purr that did the work of a whole speech.

Oakhaven’s Hearthstone Festival was nearly on them. Briar preferred calming teas and the moonpetal garden to storms or ancient wrestling. Mayor Rowan had enlisted her anyway, loud with hopeful energy. “Simple historical record-keeping. The story of the Whispering Falls. Easy enough.” She pictured sun, parchment, Ink on her lap, and said yes.

Easy arrived wearing muddle. The festival grounds were chatter and distant lutes. The History Tent was not a hush of learning. Villagers argued with passion and slightly different facts. In charge of the muddle was Quillan, an elf archivist with moonlight hair, tiny glasses, and a quill that pointed at error for a living. His voice could curdle milk with exactness.

“The Falls did not begin with a baker’s dropped pie, as young Elara believes.” Tap on the scrolls. “A celestial tear. The moon goddess wept for a lost star.”

Briar liked history the way she liked a warm biscuit: steady, with room for crumbs. Annoyance arrived gently. “Perhaps there is room for the tear and the pie.” Ink, a furry shoulder-pad, mrrped the lunch deadline.

She set a small wooden table. Ink took guard. The plan was to listen. Anyone with a memory, a whisper, a grandmother’s leftover could sit. An old shepherd, face like oak bark, swore his grandfather’s sheep had witnessed a giant eagle weeping for a lost chick. A retired weaver insisted the murmur was a lovesick sprite sighing for dawn. Quillan tutted. Fanciful. Nonsense. Scrolls rustled like offended birds.

Ink ran a quieter investigation, sniffing boots and tweed, then nudging Briar toward what she had missed. The nudge delivered her to Maeve, village elder, on a shaded bench, lined face, eyes that had kept secrets long enough to twinkle.

“They forget the great thaw of ’32.” Dry-leaf voice. “Mother told me. Ice so thick it groaned like a giant waking. When it broke, the water sang. Beautiful. Sad. That’s why we call them Whispering, child.”

Briar’s quill was halfway to the page when a playful gust — perhaps a clumsy apprentice, perhaps an actual pie — snatched Maeve’s tattered shawl. Faded colour against blue sky, heading for a thorny border bush. “My mother’s. The only thing I have from that time.”

Not a job for grand spells. Briar ran. Ink, who preferred naps, became a black blur and snagged a trailing corner a breath before the brambles claimed it. Briar took the rest. The wind, having made its joke, moved on.

Later that evening, as the many festival lights began to twinkle in the valley below like a handful of fallen stars scattered on darkening land, Briar stood before the gathered villagers with the shawl she had gently mended where a stubborn bramble had caught it. Quillan stood beside her, radiating an almost visible sense of coming criticism, quill hovering as if ready to strike. She did not offer a series of sure facts. She offered a tapestry woven from many threads.

“The archivist’s celestial tear,” she said, meeting Quillan’s gaze, “might have been ice groaning, a sound easy to file under heaven. A dropped pie can make a commotion. The truest whisper I have heard is Maeve’s mother, and the song the ice sang when spring finally won.” She held the shawl. “This travelled with that winter. It is part of the record.”

Quillan blinked. Spectacles adjusted, the sign of thought. “The exact origin of the whispering remains, of course, a scholarly subject. The story, Mistress Briar, has a certain… heartfelt truthfulness.”

Applause arrived warm, not grand. Cider, honey cakes, the murmur of people who had stopped arguing long enough to drink. Briar set a saucer of cream for Ink. His purr, after watching and shawl-work, said the cream was excellent and the day could end. Mayor Rowan, at the tent flap, looked as if easy had been a useful lie and he was not sorry. The valley lights kept their silent twinkling watch below. Briar folded the shawl back into Maeve’s hands, still warm from the mending, and did not explain what history was for. Ink finished the cream and washed a paw, which was commentary enough.
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
